one_liner: Zig @Vector(8, f64) Mandelbrot kernel 1.7x faster than 4-lane AVX intrinsics in C, because its block is twice as wide.
what_it_does: src/mandel/zig_simd/main_simd.zig is an 87-line benchmark program from ZLB, a single-author Zig-vs-C/Rust/Go/Python/Bash suite, not a library. It computes an n x n Mandelbrot grid (default 4000, max_iter 1000, x in [-2, 1], y in [-1.1, 1.1]) and prints the sum of escape-iteration counts as a checksum; no image is produced. The kernel processes eight pixels per block with @Vector(8, f64) state, a u32 lane mask and per-lane counters, under @setFloatMode(.strict).
how_it_is_fast: Masked escape-time SIMD: each block iterates z = z^2 + c on 8 lanes, ANDs the active mask with |z|^2 <= 4, adds the mask to the counters, and leaves the block when @reduce(.Or) of the mask is zero. The C and Rust SIMD rows run the identical per-lane algorithm on one 4-lane __m256d block with 64-bit counters, so the Zig version holds twice as many independent iteration chains per loop; on AVX2 hardware the 8-wide vector is split into two 256-bit chains that overlap the multiply-add latency (or one 512-bit chain on AVX-512, and the CPU is not named). The wider block even does extra work (each block runs until the slowest of 8 pixels escapes, not 4) and still wins, which points to latency-bound 4-lane C code rather than better Zig code generation; the same-algorithm scalar rows are at parity (12.374 s vs 12.386 s).
when_to_use: As a compact, MIT-licensed template for a masked escape-time loop with Zig's portable @Vector type: the kernel uses no target intrinsics, unlike the C and Rust baselines that include immintrin.h or std::arch::x86_64 and need AVX.

When choosing a block width for latency-bound SIMD loops: the suite shows an 8-lane f64 block (16 doubles of state) beating a 4-lane block by 1.7x on the same per-lane math, a lesson that applies equally to C with two __m256d chains or GCC vector extensions.
When you need bit-identical results across compilers: strict float mode in Zig and -ffp-contract=off in C keep FMA contraction out of both sides, so checksums should match the scalar versions.
As a starting point for Zig 0.16 benchmark harnesses: Makefile builds every variant, tools/runner.sh drives hyperfine and tools/aggregate.py writes the README tables and SVG plots.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Zig beats C or C++: the C kernel is 4 lanes wide and the Zig kernel 8, the scalar same-algorithm rows tie, and an 8-lane C kernel has not been measured.
Multi-core or GPU rendering: the kernel is single-threaded and writes no pixels.
Older Zig toolchains: main takes std.process.Init and writes through std.Io, the API of the Zig 0.16.0 release the README pins; it is not written for earlier releases.
Regions where neighbouring pixels escape at very different counts: every 8-pixel block runs until its slowest lane finishes, so wasted lanes grow with the block width (not measured in the repo).
As a maintained dependency: one commit (2026-08-20), 0 stars, no issues or releases.

integration.dependencies: none (Zig standard library only); the harness needs hyperfine and matplotlib
integration.platforms: Zig kernel is target-independent @Vector code built for the host CPU; measured only on Linux 7.1.4-arch, CPU not named; the C and Rust SIMD baselines are x86-64 AVX only
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded program with no shared state

gotchas: Unequal kernels behind the headline: zig_simd uses @Vector(8, f64) with u32 counters while c_simd and rust_simd use one 4-lane __m256d block with 64-bit counters; the README attributes the 1.7x to @Vector giving LLVM 'clearer intent', but the per-lane math is identical and the gap matches doubling the independent dependency chains.

Correctness is never checked during timing: runner.sh runs hyperfine with --output=null, and make test-all only prints each binary's checksum at n=100 for eyeballing, with no expected value or comparison.

runner.sh skips re-measuring any row whose binary sha256 matches the stored results/<name>.hash, so rows in results/ can come from different sessions; with a single commit there is no way to tell, and the hyperfine JSON carries no timestamps or CPU model (the README only says AVX2/AVX-512 generically).

ReleaseSafe costs about 17% on the SIMD kernel (2.249 s vs 1.922 s, derived from page data) though the README calls the cost negligible for Mandel; it is negligible only for the scalar kernel (12.393 s vs 12.374 s). The README also says all binaries are built for native, but the scalar gcc/clang and rust_std builds have no -march=native or target-cpu flag.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No sibling in this category covers Mandelbrot; like the LangArena Zig std.sort.pdq row it is a language-suite comparison rather than a library, so for production Zig code with measured wins over C libraries look at zroar (vs CRoaring) or zipir (vs zlib-ng), and use this only as a SIMD-loop example.
verified_claims_summary: Hyperfine means of 20 runs after 1 warmup (n=4000, max_iter 1000, Linux 7.1.4-arch, CPU not named): Zig 0.16.0 ReleaseFast 8-lane kernel 1.922 s (sd 0.098) vs the 4-lane AVX intrinsics C kernel at 3.302 s with gcc 16.1.1 and 3.261 s with clang 22.1.8 (both -O3 -march=native -ffp-contract=off), 3.380 s with zig cc and Rust 1.97.1 at 3.321 s, i.e. 1.70x to 1.76x (derived from page data); the scalar same-algorithm rows tie (Zig 12.374 s, gcc 12.386 s, clang 12.631 s), so the gain is block width, not language.
status_note: Single commit ('init: establish project baseline', 2026-08-20), 0 stars, MIT with REUSE metadata; small enough to copy, but it is a showcase suite tied to Zig 0.16.0 rather than a maintained library.
